title: State the event before showing a probability
text: A probability without a clear event definition is difficult to interpret. The current research target is: an observed glucose rise of at least twenty milligrams per deciliter from the latest available current reading at approximately one hundred and twenty minutes. That choice follows a declared training-only label audit. The original absolute threshold of one hundred and eighty milligrams per deciliter was eligible only if the training data contained enough positive windows, enough prevalence and positives across at least five training participants. If that support was insufficient, the declared fallback was a rise of at least twenty milligrams per deciliter, again requiring minimum support. If neither target was supported, the classifier would be disabled instead of inventing a result. The actual decision is recorded in the label audit. The research forecasts refer to approximately thirty, sixty, ninety and one hundred and twenty minutes. Ground truth is the nearest actual CGM observation within one hundred and fifty seconds of the nominal horizon, with its real timestamp retained. There is no target interpolation. If the selected event is a rise, the reference is the latest available current glucose, which can be up to fifteen minutes old. This contract differs from the old simulator's exact timestamp label and must not be conflated with it.

title: Measured research results, with their denominator
text: Here are the actual final results for the current research model. The evaluation includes 1,859 eligible windows from 3 final participants. The two-hour mean absolute error is 13.31 milligrams per deciliter. Persistence error on the same eligible windows is 16.35. The event classifier's AUROC is 0.672, average precision is 0.294, and Brier score is 0.1236. At its frozen review threshold, recall is 66.20 percent and precision is 22.14 percent. There are 97 false-negative windows and 668 false-positive windows. These are overlapping replay windows, not counts of unique clinical episodes, patients or alarms delivered to a doctor. A false-positive flag means that the defined future threshold event was not observed; it does not establish whether an intervention was necessary. The same table includes all eligible alternatives and negative controls. We present both pooled and participant-level results, along with slices and curves, because a single aggregate metric can hide uneven behavior. The comparison is exploratory, based on a small convenience dataset. It is evidence about this implementation and these recordings, not evidence of clinical effectiveness.

title: Freeze first. Reveal later. Compare honestly.
text: Challenge Lab turns the forecast into an inspectable experiment. Choose a participant, a cutoff and an available sensor case. Freeze the prediction before revealing the future. The input is physically restricted to the historical prefix, and the frozen result records the model identity, cutoff, quality state and prediction. Reveal then compares that frozen output with the original recorded observations at the requested horizons. It must not recompute the prediction after the outcome becomes available. The comparison includes persistence, error and whether the observed values fall within the forecast bands. A selected window may favor persistence, and the interface should show that result directly. The downloadable receipt makes the numerical record portable. Hashes bind the relevant model bytes and input representation so that an independent verifier can detect altered artifacts or inconsistent calculations. A hash is not a signature, an independently trusted timestamp or a clinical audit certification. The underlying dataset is publicly available, so this flow is not secure study blinding. Its value is narrower and concrete: it demonstrates that the implementation respects the prediction boundary and preserves the result it is later evaluating.

title: Test the failure boundary
text: The robustness workflow tests what happens when the observation stream becomes less trustworthy. Supported cases perturb the historical input while retaining the original reference future for comparison. That distinction prevents the model from being rewarded simply because the outcome was altered to match a perturbation. Gaps, stale readings, delay, noise and outliers test different failure modes; a missing channel is not equivalent to a systematically biased but fresh channel. The interface exposes quality dimensions and whether inference proceeds, becomes degraded or is withheld. The exact cases implemented and verified in this build are listed in the documentation and the laboratory itself. We do not claim a case is supported merely because it appeared in a design request. A particularly useful demonstration is a plausible sensor bias. It can pass a freshness check while changing the forecast, which shows why quality checks are incomplete. These perturbation results characterize software behavior under specified synthetic corruptions of recorded data. They do not prove robustness to all real devices, patient populations or clinical conditions. The jury can inspect both the numerical change and the reason given for any abstention.

title: Keep the evidence beside the experience
text: The evidence workspace is intended to make the model's limitations easy to find. It presents alternatives on the same final observations and identifies which family was actually selected. A model labelled fusion is not automatically better than CGM history alone, and the table remains visible if fusion adds little or makes error worse. The participant breakdown matters because the final set contains only three people. Horizon-specific errors show how performance changes as the forecast moves further into the future. Calibration and precision-recall views help separate ranking ability from probability quality and operating-policy consequences. Quality slices reveal whether performance differs when usable heart-rate variability is scarce or glucose coverage is reduced. These are exploratory descriptions, not independently powered subgroup studies. The prediction contract, source manifest and freeze record provide the reproducibility path behind the charts. In the demonstration, identify the current model hash, show the primary family, and compare its error with persistence. Then point to one limitation that remains unresolved. This is the central product principle: the evidence should be as accessible as the attractive forecast, including evidence that does not support a stronger claim.

title: Separate research evidence from simulator progress
text: AURA previously used a fully synthetic simulator benchmark. Those V3 results remain available as historical engineering evidence, with their model version and original cohort. The new open-research model has different data, availability rules, participants and possibly a different event target. Its recall or precision cannot be presented as an improvement over the old simulator's numbers. To address the earlier synthetic model's missed and false-positive windows, we also ran a separate experiment under the unchanged simulator and exact two-hour threshold. That experiment adds an HGB and ExtraTrees ensemble and features summarizing only prediction errors whose outcomes have already become known at the current cutoff. A past forecast does not contribute an error until its full horizon has elapsed. Candidate selection and probability calibration use separate development identities, and fresh final identities are reserved until the estimator and policy are frozen. The promotion gate requires more than a favorable threshold trade-off. The current V4 status is: On the separate fresh synthetic cohort, false-negative windows changed from 1,790 to 1,824, and false-positive windows from 7,816 to 7,329. Predeclared promotion gate failed; not promoted. These results are not comparable with the open-research model's performance.. This experiment does not modify or validate the open-research model. Keeping these evidence tracks separate prevents a change of benchmark from being mistaken for a scientific improvement.
